description: Source-lore pass 19 imports player-run organizations, organizational collapse, industrial production, and skill training.

entries.title: Player-Run Organizations
entries.summary: Guilds, companies, military factions, corporations, and townships grow through purpose, funding, infrastructure, influence, stable management, and survival under pressure.
body: Creating an organization begins with purpose, identity, structure, and goals. A guild serves a trade, a corporation pursues profit, a military faction serves power or ideology, and a township combines governance, population, law, and resources.

Funding pays for headquarters, ships, forts, staff, materials, utilities, permits, property, and political protection. Recruitment brings craftspeople, soldiers, administrators, mages, quartermasters, and specialists into the project.

Infrastructure determines where and how the organization works. Leadership may be autocratic, democratic, oligarchic, or council-based. Internal roles must manage inventory, missions, trade routes, security, diplomacy, finance, and information.

Growth requires reputation, alliances, contracts, branches, territory, patrons, taxes, or profit. Survival requires financial review, morale, diplomacy, conflict resolution, regulatory compliance, innovation, supply chains, public trust, and crisis response.
An organization shapes the world only while its people, resources, and goals remain aligned. Poor management can turn accumulated power into debt, corruption, rebellion, sabotage, and collapse.

sections.heading: Legacy Management Checks
body: The source provides six creation stages, recurring quarterly and monthly checks, setup costs, and twenty management challenges covering authority, resources, recruitment, projects, finance, morale, crises, law, innovation, supply, security, training, strategy, productivity, and customers. Conversion is required.

sourceRefs.outlineTitle: Running a large company group or Guild

entries.title: Loss of Organizational Control
entries.summary: Organizations can pass from their founders through elections, coups, rebellion, bankruptcy, sabotage, scandal, morale collapse, popular revolt, exile, or ideological schism.
body: Control can be lost peacefully through an election or violently through a coup. Military forces may rebel over mistreatment or ideology; workers may strike when bankruptcy prevents wages; rival factions may sabotage assets and routes.

Corruption scandals destroy public support. Neglect and repeated failure collapse morale. Constituents may revolt against oppression, while hostile coalitions can exile leadership and leave competing factions behind.

Ideological schism divides members into organizations with incompatible goals. The resulting loss of resources, ships, land, personnel, reputation, alliances, and political leverage may permanently change the institution even if it survives.
Founders do not automatically own an organization forever. Authority exists only while members, employees, constituents, creditors, allies, and armed forces continue to recognize it.

sections.heading: Legacy Loss-of-Control Table
body: The source gives checks and consequences for elections, coups, military rebellion, economic collapse, sabotage, scandal, morale collapse, revolt, exile, and schism. Conversion is required.

entries.title: Industrial Production
entries.summary: Production scales from a personalized solo workbench through a coordinated small team to an industrial workshop with mass output, machinery, specialists, and supply-chain risk.
body: A solo workshop supports specialized items, repairs, and low-volume craft through one worker's tools and skill. Its output is slow and personal, with failures causing imperfections, wasted material, and delay.
A small team divides work among assistants with complementary skills. Leadership and task allocation improve speed and material use, but mismanagement spreads errors across the whole batch.

An industrial workshop uses dozens of workers, steam hammers, presses, looms, enchanted crystal machinery, specialized stations, and large material stocks. Management becomes as important as craft skill because breakdowns, low morale, and supply disruption can stop production entirely.

High-quality management can improve finish, durability, enchantment stability, material efficiency, output, reputation, and profit. Scaling production therefore creates power and vulnerability together.

sections.heading: Legacy Production Tiers
body: The source gives skill DCs, staff counts, item output per week, batch times, and failure outcomes for solo, small-team, and industrial production. Conversion is required.

entries.title: Skill Training and Instruction
entries.summary: Characters can gain skills through formal lessons, apprenticeships, private instructors, mentors, or guild programs that require time, money, practice, access, and assessment.
body: Training begins by choosing a skill and locating an appropriate teacher, school, guild, or academy. Common skills are widely available, while magic, rare crafts, dragon lore, and advanced techniques may require unique instructors or political access.

Students attend lessons and practice over weeks or months. Progress depends on participation, comprehension, instructor quality, and the complexity of the subject. Failed sessions waste time and money or require remedial work.
A final practical assessment determines whether the student gains proficiency or deeper expertise. Failure may require additional lessons or restarting part of the course.

Mentorships exchange lower cost and personal guidance for slower, less structured progress. Guild training offers established facilities and curriculum but may demand membership fees, labor, service, favors, or guild-specific quests.

sections.heading: Legacy Training Economy
body: The source gives daily gold costs, training durations, instructor-search checks, weekly progression, final assessments, and categories for basic, crafting, weapon, magical, social, and rare skills. Conversion is required.
